verses.zh: 山岩间的野山羊几时生产，你知道吗？母鹿下犊之期，你能察定吗？
verses.en: “Are you acquainted with the way[NOTE:1] the mountain goats[NOTE:2] give birth?Do you watch as the wild deer give birth to their young?
notes: The text uses the infinitive as the object: “do you know the giving birth of?”
Or “ibex.”
verses.commentary:
39:1-4 This strophe relates to questions about how and when animals give
birth to their young.

- ibex (NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 488)

- deer

verses.zh: 它们怀胎的月数，你能数算吗？它们几时生产，你能晓得吗？
verses.en: Do you count the months they must fulfill,and do you know the time they give birth?[NOTE:1]
notes: Here the infinitive is again a substantive: “the time of their giving birth.”

verses.zh: 它们屈身，将子生下，就除掉疼痛。
verses.en: They crouch; they bear[NOTE:1] their young;they bring forth the offspring they have carried.[NOTE:2]
notes: The Hebrew verb used here means “to cleave,” and this would not have the object “their young.” Olshausen and others after him change the ח (khet) to ט (tet) and get a verb “to drop,” meaning “drop [= give birth to] young” as used in Job 21:10. G. R. Driver holds out for the MT, arguing it is an idiom, “to breach the womb” (“Problems in the Hebrew text of Job,” VTSup 3 [1955]: 92-93).

Heb “they cast forth their labor pains.” This word usually means “birth pangs” but here can mean what caused the pains (metonymy of effect). This fits better with the parallelism, and the verb (“cast forth”). The words “their offspring” are supplied in the translation for clarity; direct objects were often omitted when clear from the context, although English expects them to be included.
verses.commentary:
39:3 "labor pains" AB
(p. 259) suggests that the root is not MT (BDB 286, KB 286), which
denotes pain in birth, but an Arabic root that denotes rapid birth.

verses.zh: 这子渐渐肥壮，在荒野长大，去而不回。
verses.en: Their young grow strong and grow up in the open;[NOTE:1] they go off and do not return to them.
notes: The idea is that of the open countryside. The Aramaism is found only here.
verses.commentary:
39:4 "the open field"
The MT has "in the open field" (BDB 141, KB 153 IV), which is
found only here in the OT. The root is either from Arabic or Aramaic
(this verse has possibly three Aramaic roots). It denotes uninhabited,
uncultivated land.

verses.zh: 谁放野驴出去自由？谁解开快驴的绳索？
verses.en: Who let the wild donkey go free?Who released the bonds of the donkey,
verses.commentary:
39:5-12 This strophe deals with
questions about animals which are hard to domesticate.

- wild donkey

- wild ox (cf. Num. 23:22; 24:8; Deut. 33:17; Ps. 22:21; 29:6)

- LXX, "unicorn"

- Vulgate, "rhinoceros"

- AB, "buffalo" (avroch)

39:5 "swift donkey"
This NOUN (BDB 789, KB
882) is found only here in the OT. It is possibly an Aramaic root
(NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 531).

SPECIAL TOPIC: MULES AND DONKEYS

verses.zh: 我使旷野作它的住处，使咸地当它的居所。
verses.en: to whom I appointed the arid rift valley[NOTE:1] for its home,the salt wastes as its dwelling place?
notes: See the note at Job 24:5.

verses.zh: 它嗤笑城内的喧嚷，不听赶牲口的喝声。
verses.en: It scorns the tumult in the town;it does not hear the shouts of a driver.[NOTE:1]
notes: The animal is happier in open countryside than in a busy town, and on its own rather than being driven by a herdsman.

verses.zh: 遍山是它的草场；它寻找各样青绿之物。
verses.en: It ranges the hills as its pastureand searches after every green plant.

verses.zh: 野牛岂肯服事你？岂肯住在你的槽旁？
verses.en: Is the wild ox willing to be your servant?Will it spend the night at your feeding trough?

verses.zh: 你岂能用套绳将野牛笼在犁沟之间？它岂肯随你耙山谷之地？
verses.en: Can you bind the wild ox[NOTE:1] to a furrow with its rope;will it till the valleys, following after you?
notes: Some commentators think that the addition of the “wild ox” here is a copyist’s error, making the stich too long. They therefore delete it. Also, binding an animal to the furrow with ropes is unusual. So with a slight emendation Kissane came up with “Will you bind him with a halter of cord?” While the MT is unusual, the sense is understandable, and no changes, even slight ones, are absolutely necessary.

verses.zh: 岂可因它的力大就倚靠它？岂可把你的工交给它做吗？
verses.en: Will you rely on it because its strength is great?Will you commit[NOTE:1] your labor to it?
notes: Heb “leave.”

verses.zh: 岂可信靠它把你的粮食运到家，又收聚你禾场上的谷吗？
verses.en: Can you count[NOTE:1] on it to bring in[NOTE:2] your grain[NOTE:3] and gather the grain[NOTE:4] to your threshing floor?[NOTE:5]
notes: The word is normally translated “believe” in the Bible. The idea is that of considering something dependable and acting on it. The idea of reliability is found also in the Niphal stem usages.

There is a textual problem here: יָשׁוּב (yashuv) is the Kethib, meaning “[that] he will return”; יָשִׁיב (yashiv) is the Qere, meaning “that he will bring in.” This is the preferred reading, since the object follows it. For commentators who think the line too unbalanced for this, the object is moved to the second colon, and the reading “returns” is taken for the first. But the MT is perfectly clear as it stands.
Heb “your seed”; this must be interpreted figuratively for what the seed produces.
Heb “gather it”; the referent (the grain) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Simply, the MT has “and your threshing floor gather.” The “threshing floor” has to be an adverbial accusative of place.

verses.zh: 鸵鸟的翅膀欢然搧展，岂是显慈爱的翎毛和羽毛吗？
verses.en: [NOTE:1] “The wings of the ostrich[NOTE:2] flap with joy,[NOTE:3] but are they the pinions and plumage of a stork?[NOTE:4]
notes: This whole section on the ostrich is not included in the LXX. Many feel it is an interpolation and should therefore be deleted. The pattern of the chapter changes from the questions being asked to observations being made.
The word occurs only here and means “shrill cries.” If the MT is correct, this is a poetic name for the ostrich (see Lam 4:3).
Many proposals have been made here. The MT has a verb, “exult.” Strahan had “flap joyously,” a rendering followed by the NIV. The RSV uses “wave proudly.”

The point of this statement would be that the ostrich cannot compare to the stork. But there are many other proposals for this line—just about every commentator has a different explanation for it. Of the three words here, the first means “pinion,” the third “plumage,” and the second probably “stork,” although the LXX has “heron.” The point of this whole section is that the ostrich is totally lacking in parental care, whereas the stork is characterized by it. The Hebrew word for “stork” is the same word for “love”: חֲסִידָה (khasidah), an interpretation followed by the NASB. The most likely reading is “or are they the pinions and plumage of the stork?” The ostrich may flap about, but cannot fly and does not care for its young.

verses.zh: 因它把蛋留在地上，在尘土中使得温暖；
verses.en: For she leaves[NOTE:1] her eggs on the groundand lets them be warmed on the soil.
notes: The meaning may have the connotation of “lays; places,” rather than simply abandoning (see M. Dahood, “The Root ʿzb II in Job,” JBL 78 [1959]: 307f.).

verses.zh: 却想不到被脚踹碎，或被野兽践踏。
verses.en: She forgets that a foot might crush themor that a wild animal[NOTE:1] might trample them.
notes: Heb “an animal of the field.”

verses.zh: 它忍心待雏，似乎不是自己的；虽然徒受劳苦，也不为雏惧怕；
verses.en: She is harsh[NOTE:1] with her young, as if they were not hers;she is unconcerned about the uselessness of her labor.
notes: This verb, “to deal harshly; to harden; to treat cruelly,” is used for hardening the heart elsewhere (see Isa 63:17).

verses.zh: 因为　神使它没有智慧，也未将悟性赐给它。
verses.en: For God deprived her of wisdomand did not impart understanding to her.

verses.zh: 它几时挺身展开翅膀，就嗤笑马和骑马的人。
verses.en: But as soon as she springs up,[NOTE:1] she laughs at the horse and its rider.
notes: The colon poses a slight problem here. The literal meaning of the Hebrew verb translated “springs up” (i.e., “lifts herself on high”) might suggest flight. But some of the proposals involve a reading about readying herself to run.
verses.commentary:
39:18 This verse denotes the
birds' ability to rapidly rise and flee hunters. The
VERB in Job 39:18a is found only
here in the OT; possibly "flap the wings" or "beat the
air" (BDB 597, KB 630, Hiphil PERFECT).

verses.zh: 马的大力是你所赐的吗？它颈项上挓挲的鬃是你给它披上的吗？
verses.en: “Do you give the horse its strength?Do you clothe its neck with a mane?[NOTE:1]
notes: The second half of the verse contains this hapax legomenon, which is usually connected with the word רַעְמָה (raʿmah, “thunder”). A. B. Davidson thought it referred to the quivering of the neck rather than the mane. Gray thought the sound and not the movement was the point. But without better evidence, a reading that has “quivering mane” may not be far off the mark. But it may be simplest to translate it “mane” and assume that the idea of “quivering” is part of the meaning.
verses.commentary:
39:19-25 This strophe is about
the war horse. It is the only domesticated animal in the list. It was
used for hunting, war, and as a regal mount for leaders.

verses.zh: 是你叫它跳跃像蝗虫吗？它喷气之威使人惊惶。
verses.en: Do you make it leap[NOTE:1] like a locust?Its proud neighing[NOTE:2] is terrifying!
notes: The same ideas are found in Joel 2:4. The leaping motion is compared to the galloping of the horse.
The word could mean “snorting” as well (see Jer 8:16). It comes from the root “to blow.” If the horse is running and breathing hard, this could be the sense here.
verses.commentary:
39:20 Locusts and horses are
often compared (cf. Jer. 51:27; Joel 2:4; Rev. 9:7).

39:21a

NASB, NKJV, NJB, Net
"paws in the valley"

NRSV
"paws violently"

JPSOA
"paws with force"

LXX, Peshitta
"paws in the plain"

REB
"paws and prances"

The MT has "valley" (BDB 770, KB 847 I), but several scholars
think the basic root is parallel to "strength" (BDB 470) in
line b (NRSV, JPSOA). This fits the parallelism best.

verses.zh: 它在谷中刨地，自喜其力；它出去迎接佩带兵器的人。
verses.en: It[NOTE:1] paws the ground in the valley,[NOTE:2] exulting mightily;[NOTE:3] it goes out to meet the weapons.
notes: The Hebrew text has a plural verb, “they paw.” For consistency and for stylistic reasons this is translated as a singular.

The armies would prepare for battles that were usually fought in the valleys, and so the horse was ready to charge. But in Ugaritic the word ʿmk means “force” as well as “valley.” The idea of “force” would fit the parallelism here well (see M. Dahood, “Value of Ugaritic for textual criticism,” Bib 40 [1959]: 166).
Or “in strength.”

verses.zh: 它嗤笑可怕的事并不惊惶，也不因刀剑退回。
verses.en: It laughs at fear and is not dismayed;it does not shy away from the sword.

verses.zh: 箭袋和发亮的枪，并短枪在它身上铮铮有声。
verses.en: On it the quiver rattles;the lance and javelin[NOTE:1] flash.
notes: This may be the scimitar (see G. Molin, “What is a kidon?” JSS 1 [1956]: 334-37).
verses.commentary:
39:23 "rattles" This
VERB (BDB 943, KB 1246, Qal
IMPERFECT) occurs only here. It denotes
the sound of battle implements that were hung on the
warhorses, making a clanking sound as the horse runs.

verses.zh: 它发猛烈的怒气将地吞下；一听角声就不耐站立。
verses.en: In excitement and impatience it consumes the ground;[NOTE:1] it cannot stand still[NOTE:2] when the trumpet is blown.
notes: “Swallow the ground” is a metaphor for the horse’s running. Gray renders the line: “quivering and excited he dashes into the fray.”

The use of אָמַן (ʾaman) in the Hiphil in this place is unique. Such a form would normally mean “to believe.” But its basic etymological meaning comes through here. The verb means “to be firm; to be reliable; to be dependable.” The causative here would mean “to make firm” or “to stand firm.”

verses.zh: 角每发声，它说呵哈；它从远处闻着战气，又听见军长大发雷声和兵丁呐喊。
verses.en: At the sound of the trumpet, it says, ‘Aha!’And from a distance it catches the scent of battle,the thunderous shouting of commanders, and the battle cries.

verses.zh: 鹰雀飞翔，展开翅膀一直向南，岂是藉你的智慧吗？
verses.en: “Is it by your understanding that the hawk soars[NOTE:1] and spreads its wings toward the south?
notes: This word occurs only here. It is connected to “pinions” in v. 13. Dhorme suggests “clad with feathers,” but the line suggests more the use of the wings.
verses.commentary:
39:26-30 This strophe is about
the hawk (Job 39:26) and eagle/vulture (Job 39:27-30).

39:26 "the south" This could refer to

- soaring on the south wind

- an annual migration to the south

39:30b This imagery is used in NT
prophecy (cf. Matt. 24:28; Luke 17:37).

verses.zh: 大鹰上腾在高处搭窝，岂是听你的吩咐吗？
verses.en: Is it at your command[NOTE:1] that the eagle soarsand builds its nest on high?
notes: Heb “your mouth.”

verses.zh: 它住在山岩，以山峰和坚固之所为家，
verses.en: It lives on a rock and spends the night there,on a rocky crag[NOTE:1] and a fortress.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “upon the tooth of a rock.”
The word could be taken as the predicate, but because of the conjunction it seems to be adding another description of the place of its nest.

verses.zh: 从那里窥看食物，眼睛远远观望。
verses.en: From there it spots[NOTE:1] its prey;[NOTE:2] its eyes gaze intently from a distance.
notes: The word means “search,” but can be used for a wide range of matters, including spying.
Heb “food.”

verses.zh: 它的雏也咂血；被杀的人在哪里，它也在那里。
verses.en: And its young ones devour the blood,and where the dead carcasses[NOTE:1] are, there it is.”
notes: The word חֲלָלִים (khalalim) designates someone who is fatally wounded, literally the “pierced one,” meaning anyone or thing that dies a violent death.

Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- As Job 38:1-38 dealt with questions about the creation of the
physical planet, Job 38:39-40:30 deals with questions about the earth's
animal life.

- In the list of animals in this chapter, there is an implied contrast (NASB Study
Bible, p. 731) between

- domesticated donkeys and wild donkeys

- domesticated oxen and wild oxen

- The strophe about the ostrich (i.e., Job 38:13-18) is unique in that God does
not ask Job a question about its actions. Also, its actions seem strange,
therefore God does not give this animal natural wisdom, as He does the
other animals mentioned.

It is missing in the LXX, which has caused some scholars (Jerome Biblical
Commentary) to suggest it is a later addition to the text of Job. However, the LXX
often omits lines of difficult Hebrew texts (Expositor's Bible Commentary,
vol. 4, pp. 1039,1043).
